philology.title: What is Sheol? Is it hell?
philology.summary: Myers argues that sheol, used sixty-six times in the Hebrew Scriptures, simply means grave or pit: a hole in the ground where bodies are laid. Righteous and wicked alike go there, and no Old Testament text describes it as a place of afterlife torment. Since sheol is the only possible Old Testament term for hell, he concludes the Old Testament teaches nothing about hell, and asks why a loving God would never have warned anyone about it.
points: Both good and evil people go to sheol, as Genesis 37:35, Numbers 16:30 and Jonah 2:2 show, so it cannot match the modern idea of hell.
The Hebrew word bor, literally a hole dug in the ground, is often used as a synonym for sheol, as in Isaiah 14:11-20.
Like any grave, sheol is marked by worms and decay (Job 17:13-16; 24:19-20), and is described as wet, dark, dusty and musty.
When New Testament authors quote sheol texts such as Psalm 16:10 and Hosea 13:14, they connect them to bodily resurrection from the grave (Acts 2:27; 1 Corinthians 15:55).
Used metaphorically, sheol can stand for depression, sorrow or loneliness, emotions associated with death and burial: being cut off from the life God desires.
If billions faced eternal torment, the Hebrew Scriptures' total silence would mean God never warned them; Myers concludes the warning was unnecessary because the disaster does not exist.
philology.differs: The existing explanation calls Sheol a realm of the dead where all sleep; Myers reduces it further to the literal grave and denies it describes any afterlife experience at all.

quote.text: There is not a single Old Testament text which speaks of sheol as an eternal place of suffering and torment for the unregenerate dead.

philology.title: What is Hades in the Bible? Is it hell?
philology.summary: Myers argues that hades, the Septuagint's usual translation of sheol, starts as the grave, but in the New Testament mainly names the power of despair, decay and destruction that enslaves people in this life. Capernaum being brought down to hades, the gates of hades, and Death riding with hades all point to present earthly realities, and at the end death and hades are thrown into the Lake of Fire.
points: In Jesus' day Pharisees imagined the dead awaiting resurrection in compartments of one realm (Josephus), but telling the rich man and Lazarus story does not mean Jesus endorsed that picture.
Capernaum exalted to heaven and brought down to hades (Matthew 11:23; Luke 10:15) refers to the city's historical loss of power and destruction, not its citizens' eternal torment.
In Matthew 16:18 the church attacks the gates of hades, so hades exists here and now, holding people captive whom Jesus' church sets free.
The Greek god Hades was sometimes depicted with a key to the underworld; in Revelation 1:18 Jesus now holds the keys of death and hades to throw the gates open.
In Revelation 6:8 Death is the only rider without a weapon; hades itself is the instrument by which he brings death on the world.
Throwing death and hades into the Lake of Fire (Revelation 20:13-14) makes sense only if they are destructive powers, not places.
philology.differs: The existing explanation treats Hades as a temporary holding place of the dead; Myers grants that first-century view but argues Jesus mainly used hades for a destructive power at work in this life.

quote.text: Hadēs is here and now, and Jesus leads to the church to set free those who trapped behind its bars.

tartarus.title: Do the words Abyss or Tartarus refer to hell?
tartarus.summary: Myers argues that neither the abyss nor Tartarus describes hell. The abyss translates the Hebrew tehom, the deep sea, a symbol of chaos opposing God's order. Tartarus, used once in 2 Peter 2:4, alludes to Greek myth without endorsing it, and its chains of darkness most likely picture the fear fallen angels feel as they await judgment. Either way, Scripture never says any human is sent there.
points: Abussos means bottomless; in the Septuagint it translates tehom, the deep, an ancient and menacing word for chaos arrayed against creation (Genesis 1:2).
In Revelation the beast rises from the sea or abyss, symbolizing chaos, and is finally sent back there, as Jesus sent demons into the deep (Luke 8:31; Revelation 20:1-3).
No reference to the abyss ever describes fire, suffering or the eternal torture of people; going down into it pictures death in the depths of the sea.
In Greek myth some of the worst humans, such as Sisyphus and Tantalus, were sent to Tartarus, yet Peter alludes to the myth without endorsing it, as Christians mention Cupid's arrows.
Myers weighs two readings, a primeval angelic rebellion or the sons of God in Genesis 6, but both clash with evil spirits still active in the Gospels and Satan still prowling.
Wisdom of Solomon 17 calls the ninth plague of darkness on Egypt a chain of darkness, a prison not made of iron; Peter appears to draw on that imagery.
tartarus.differs: The existing explanation already covers the myth, the symbolic chains and the absence of humans; Myers adds a parallel study of the abyss as the chaotic deep sea.

quote.text: Whatever Tartarus is, humans do not experience it at all.

gehenna.title: What is Gehenna? Is it hell?
gehenna.summary: Myers argues that Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom southwest of Jerusalem, was in Jesus' day the city dump, filled with refuse and corpses, smoldering day and night, and haunted by scavenging lepers. Because it is a place name it should not be translated as hell. Jesus and James used it symbolically, he says, to warn of a hellish, destroyed life now, not burning in the next life.
points: The bodies of 185,000 Assyrian soldiers were piled and burned in the valley in Hezekiah's day (Isaiah 30:31-33; 37:36), and Jeremiah warned Israel of the same fate.
Because more garbage was added daily, the dump's fire never really died, and where flames missed, worms and maggots consumed refuse and corpses.
Myers asks readers to imagine taking out the trash: acrid smoke, a blood-red sun, half-burned corpses, and lepers scavenging for food.
We do not translate Jerusalem as City of Peace or Bethel as City of God, so Gehenna should stay Gehenna or be rendered the Valley of Hinnom.
People sent to the valley, usually for crime or leprosy, lost family and friends; Jesus' warnings aim to keep us from destroying our health, relationships and reputation.
Myers quotes N. T. Wright: Jesus warned that unless Israel abandoned armed revolt, Rome would turn Jerusalem into an extension of its smoldering rubbish heap.
gehenna.differs: Myers stresses a burning city dump and scavenging lepers, a detail the existing explanation does not rely on, and reads the warnings as personal ruin in this life as well as national judgment.

quote.text: When Jesus speaks about gehenna, He is not warning about hell in the next life, but a hellish existence in this life.

gehenna.title: Is the everlasting fire of Matthew 18:8-9 a reference to everlasting torment in hell?
gehenna.summary: Myers argues that the everlasting fire of Matthew 18:8-9 is Gehenna's dump fire, which burned day and night. Lepers survived by scavenging there, and some, at the first sign of leprosy on a hand or foot, would rather cut it off and live maimed than be diagnosed and sent to Gehenna. Jesus is teaching that sin has destructive consequences in this life and sometimes requires drastic cuts, not warning of afterlife torture.
points: Lepers often lost body parts through infection, amputation or accident; a numb foot could burn in a night fire and need amputation.
A rotting, injured eye was better removed than left to spread corruption through the body, which could eventually land a person in Gehenna.
The application: a person infected with the rot of addiction or bad influences should cut those places or people out of life before the damage spreads.
The surrounding chapter shows how: cut out pride (Matthew 18:1-5), seek the lost sheep, separate from the unrepentant, and forgive debts (Matthew 18:21-35).
The point of the whole context is that it is better to go through this life without pride or certain friends than to lose yourself, family and finances.
gehenna.differs: The existing explanation reads cutting off the eye as hyperbole about lustful thought; Myers reads it against literal leprosy and amputation at the dump, applied to cutting off destructive influences.

quote.text: Matthew 18:8-9 is not a warning about everlasting punishment in hell, but is rather a warning about the experience of a hellish life here and now.

lakeoffire.title: What is the Lake of Fire in the Bible? Is it hell?
lakeoffire.summary: Myers argues that the Lake of Fire was the Dead Sea, a place that once erupted with tar, smoke, sulfur and flame and into which Jews cast idolatrous things. As a symbol it means being banished, never heard from again. Devil, beast, false prophet, death and hades are perverted powers discarded like counterfeit coins. People sent there are not tormented; they escape the convicting presence of Jesus into a self-chosen, endless existence apart from God.
points: Philo, Strabo, Diodorus and Josephus describe fires, sulfur stench and smoking ruins around the Dead Sea; the Greeks called it Lake Asphaltites.
The Talmud says vessels bearing images of the sun, moon or a dragon should be cast into the salt sea, echoing Revelation 21:8.
After 70 AD, corpses burned in the Valley of Hinnom washed down the Wadi an-Nar, the Streambed of Fire, into the Dead Sea.
Sodom, Gomorrah and Jerusalem were burned yet will be restored (Ezekiel 16:53-55; 47:1-12), but what is cast into the Lake of Fire has no restoration.
Basanizo means rubbing on a touchstone that exposes counterfeit coins; in Revelation 20:10 only the devil, beast and false prophet, powers not people, are tormented.
Torment in Revelation 14:10 happens in the presence of the Lamb, like the witnesses' preaching that tormented hearers (Revelation 11:10): the vexation of truth, not fire.
Like C. S. Lewis' The Great Divorce, the second death is endless life apart from God without death's escape, a hell of people's own making.
lakeoffire.differs: The existing explanation reads the lake as a refining crucible that purifies and may restore all; Myers sees no restoration for what is cast in, and an eternal, self-chosen separated existence for people.

quote.text: They are not in torment there, but are sent there to escape their torment.

darkness.title: What is the Outer Darkness in the Bible? Is it hell?
darkness.summary: Myers argues that the three outer darkness passages in Matthew describe exclusion from a lit celebration, not hell. In Matthew 8:12 and 22:13 unfaithful believers, still possessing eternal life, miss the inaugural feast when Jesus returns and weep with shame and regret. In Matthew 25:30 he reads it as the greedy master's verdict, casting an honorable servant into society's dark margins. Weeping and gnashing of teeth is an idiom of sorrow over a missed blessing.
points: Those cast out in Matthew 8:12 are called sons of the kingdom, a title for kingdom citizens, not unregenerate people bound for hell.
Hosts commonly supplied wedding garments (Judges 14:12), so the underdressed guest refused the king's provision; his presence at the feast shows he was a believer.
Zane Hodges notes there are no torturers in the darkness; being bound hand and foot pictures exclusion and limitation, not torment.
Like Scrooge peering through a window at a warm Christmas party, some Christians will watch the celebration from the dark street.
Kingdom of heaven is added by translators in Matthew 25:14; in an honor-shame culture the profit-making servants were exploiters and the third servant acted honorably.
The shame and regret do not last: after the Wedding Feast of the Lamb every tear is wiped away (Revelation 19:6-9; 21:4).
darkness.differs: Myers agrees the darkness is outside a lit feast, but reads Matthew 25:30 as the worldly master's punishment of an honorable servant who refused his greedy system, not as God's verdict.

quote.text: When Jesus returns, He will throw a party full of lights, music, feasting, and dancing. But not all Christians will get to experience this party.

weddingfeast.title: What is the Outer Darkness in the Bible? Is it hell?
weddingfeast.summary: Myers argues that Matthew 22:13 clearly concerns exclusion from the wedding feast, not hell. The underdressed guest was inside the hall, so he was a believer; he refused the garment the host provided and wore his own clothes. His removal is discipline: he keeps eternal life but misses the inauguration celebration when Jesus returns, standing outside the lights in shame and regret.
points: Many scholars note hosts in Middle-Eastern and Mediterranean cultures supplied guests' garments (Judges 14:12), so poverty or ignorance was no excuse.
The man thought his own clothes were fine and did not need the king's; Myers links the garment to righteous living, quoting Gregory Sapaugh.
Only believers could enter the feast, so an unbeliever could not have been there; eternal salvation, Sapaugh says, is not at issue.
Joshua Ryan Butler pictures prodigals and prostitutes partying inside while the self-righteous, who thought their own clothes good enough, weep outside.
Zane Hodges says being tied hand and foot means exclusion and limited activity, not torture, and that exclusion concerns co-reigning with Christ.
weddingfeast.differs: The existing explanation reads the expelled guest within Israel's refusal of the Messiah; Myers treats him as a genuine but unfaithful believer who keeps eternal life and only misses the opening celebration.

quote.text: The fact that this man is at the wedding feast proves that he is a genuine believer, for only believers are welcomed into the feast.

talents.title: What is the Outer Darkness in the Bible? Is it hell?
talents.summary: Myers notes the common reading, that the unprofitable servant is a believer who misses the kingdom's opening feast, but prefers another. The master who travels to a far country resembles Herod and acts as an exploiter by first-century honor-shame values. The third servant refused his greedy scheme, so the outer darkness of Matthew 25:30 is the rich lord's verdict: banishment from his household's party to the dark streets, not hell.
points: The words kingdom of heaven in Matthew 25:14 are added by translators; Jesus describes the kingdom in the surrounding parables, while this one contrasts the kingdom of this world.
In a zero-sum honor-shame culture, anyone suddenly acquiring more was judged a thief (John Pilch), so the two profitable servants imitated their exploiting master.
Malina and Rohrbaugh say that from the peasant point of view the third servant acted honorably by refusing the greedy rich man's schemes.
Luke's version follows Zacchaeus, who gave away wealth gained by exploitation and likely lost friends, status and invitations to fancy parties.
The Sheep and the Goats then shows that those rejected by worldly kingdoms are honored in God's kingdom, echoing Matthew 6:24 on God and money.
talents.differs: The existing explanation casts the master as the returning king and the darkness as exclusion from his feast; Myers sees the master as a Herod-like exploiter and the third servant as the honorable one.

quote.text: He passed up the deal of a lifetime, and will live to regret it.
